name: encoding-utf8
algorithm: Lossy UTF-8 decode of mostly valid text: a mixed-script line (ASCII, Latin-1, Cyrillic, CJK, one astral scalar) repeated n times with one lone 0xFF about every 997 bytes, rounds times, each language's standard decoder writing U+FFFD for each 0xFF; the checksum adds per round the output length and one output byte at a moving index (README.md).

skip.c: no lossy UTF-8 decoder in C's standard library
skip.mk-wrap: the checksum already uses the wrapping operators; the task has no other arithmetic to wrap

no_counts: B24 does not apply: an idiomatic row compares libraries; the decoder is tested by the lane's Go tests (TestStdEncoding_WptCases, TestStdEncoding_DecodeAdversarial)
notes: Every column allocates its output afresh each round and frees it (std-encoding fix round, 2026-11-12: before it Mk reset one arena and Zig reused one buffer, so their output landed on warm pages while Rust and Go allocated). Mk: encoding.Utf8.Decode into a new Arena each round, freed at its end (sized in one pass, written in a second: Mk's API). Rust: String::from_utf8_lossy, an owned String each round. Zig: std.unicode.fmtUtf8 printed into a fixed Writer over a buffer allocated and freed each round. Go: strings.ToValidUTF8 with U+FFFD, a new string each round.

Each 0xFF replaces an ASCII byte, so it stands alone among valid scalars and every decoder writes one U+FFFD for it: the WHATWG decoder (maximal subparts: Mk, Rust, Zig) and Go's ToValidUTF8 (one U+FFFD per run of invalid bytes) agree.
Checksums: Go's at both sizes on the owner's machine (std-encoding session 2, 2026-11-12); tools/bench verify checks the other columns.
Not published: no number here is a measurement.
